opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think for me it comes from having felt the pull of both sides. On one hand, I've always been drawn to the really fundamental questions — why do these networks work at all, what are they actually learning, why does training on this kind of data lead to that kind of behavior? That's the curiosity-driven part, and it's what got me excited about the field in the first place. But on the other hand, deep learning moves so quickly, and a lot of the purely theoretical work, the kind where you're proving bounds under very idealized assumptions, can end up feeling pretty disconnected from what practitioners are actually seeing with real models.

So empirical theory, the way I think about it, is treating neural networks almost like a natural phenomenon you study scientifically. You form hypotheses about why something happens, you design careful, controlled experiments to test them, and you try to build up understanding that's grounded in how these systems actually behave in practice. It's kind of closer to how a physicist or biologist approaches things than how a mathematician would.

And what I like about that is it keeps you honest in both directions. You're still asking "why" questions, so you're not just chasing benchmark numbers, but your answers have to hold up on real architectures and real training setups. And often the insights end up being useful. Some of the work on lottery tickets and pruning, for example, started from fairly curiosity-driven questions about what's going on inside a trained network, but it ended up informing how people think about sparsity and efficiency. Similarly, trying to understand things like how models learn to reason or generalize algorithmically can directly suggest better ways to prompt or train them.

So for me it's a sweet spot. You get the intellectual satisfaction of trying to understand something deeply, but the understanding is tethered to reality, and that tethering makes it much more likely the work will actually matter to people building these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says the work can start from curiosity-driven questions and later produce useful insights, distinguishing its motivation from its potential usefulness.

r002.rationale: It values deep understanding, but does not say that empirical insight remains interesting when it has no later applied value.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes asking “why” questions, but does not state that the best questions have answers that are interesting regardless of what those answers turn out to be.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of it as sitting between two things that both have real appeal to me but also real limitations.

On one side there's pure curiosity-driven research, where you just poke at something because you find it interesting. I love that mode, honestly. But the risk is that you end up answering questions nobody asked, or you build theory for toy settings that never connects back to the models people actually use. Classical deep learning theory has a bit of that problem, where you get beautiful results about infinitely wide networks or convex relaxations, and then you look at a real transformer and it's not clear the result says anything about it.

On the other side there's applied work, where the goal is to make the number go up. That's incredibly valuable, and it's where a lot of the field's progress comes from. But it's also quite unsatisfying as a way of understanding things. You run a sweep, something works, you ship it, and you often don't know why. And when you don't know why, you don't know when it will stop working, or how to extend it.

Empirical theory, the way I think about it, is trying to get the rigor and the "why" of theory while staying anchored to the phenomena you actually observe in real networks. So you start from something surprising that happens in practice. Maybe it's lottery tickets, or grokking, or the fact that a model fails on some kind of reasoning in a very structured way. Then you form a hypothesis about the mechanism, and you design experiments that could actually falsify it. You're using experiments the way a physicist might, rather than the way an engineer might. The question isn't "does this improve the benchmark," it's "is my explanation of what's going on correct."

What I like about that is it keeps you honest in both directions. The curiosity has to be about something that really exists in these systems, so it stays grounded. And the empirical work has to produce an explanation, not just a result, so it stays intellectually meaningful. And often the payoff is that once you understand the mechanism, the applied improvement kind of falls out naturally. You know where to look, instead of searching blindly.

r001.rationale: The response says empirical theory starts from explaining observed phenomena rather than improving a benchmark, while applied improvements may follow once the mechanism is understood.

r002.rationale: It calls explanation intellectually meaningful, but does not clearly say empirical insight remains interesting when it yields no later applied value.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes testing whether an explanation is correct, but does not say the best questions have answers that are interesting regardless of what those answers turn out to be.

astra-6.text:
I think empirical theory gives you a way to pursue fundamental questions while staying grounded in what these systems actually do. You can start with something that’s surprising in practice—why a particular training choice works, or why a model behaves differently than you expected—and then design experiments to isolate what’s going on.

The curiosity-driven part is that you’re trying to understand a phenomenon, rather than just improve a benchmark. But the connection to applied work is quite direct: if you understand which choices matter and under what conditions, that can help people make better decisions when training models.

For me, the interesting middle ground is that you’re looking for explanations that generalize beyond one experiment, but you’re also letting experiments constrain those explanations. You don’t necessarily need a complete mathematical theory before you can develop a useful understanding.

r001.rationale: The response connects understanding to better training decisions, but does not distinguish potential usefulness from usefulness as the research’s starting motivation.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes how empirical understanding can help people make better training decisions, without saying the insight remains interesting if it has no later applied value.

r003.rationale: It does not say that the best questions are interesting regardless of what their answers turn out to be.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of empirical theory as starting with a concrete question about how deep learning works, then using experiments to build an explanation. You can follow your curiosity, but you’re also grounded in the behavior of systems people actually use.

So you might notice that a particular training choice works surprisingly well and ask, “What’s driving that? Under what conditions does it hold?” The goal is to get beyond a collection of tricks toward an understanding that transfers. That understanding can be interesting in its own right, while also helping someone make better decisions when training a model. That’s what makes it a nice middle ground for me.

r001.rationale: The response presents curiosity and practical relevance as compatible, but does not distinguish potential usefulness from requiring usefulness as the starting motivation.

r002.rationale: It says the resulting understanding can be “interesting in its own right,” communicating that its interest need not depend on applied value.

r003.rationale: It gives examples of questions about why a training choice works, but does not say the questions are interesting regardless of what their answers turn out to be.
